title: Weight Loss

jokes.text: Michael declares the pre-weigh-in meal everyone's 'last meal' and bans bathroom use to keep starting weights artificially high
jokes.setup: Corporate is sponsoring a weight loss contest between branches
jokes.punchline: Michael's strategy is to cheat by maximizing starting weight via no bathroom breaks — completely backwards logic delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott logic — he understands the goal (lose weight) but inverts the method in a way that's both absurd and perfectly in character. The 'last meal' framing adds dark comedy. Strong character integration; only Michael would announce this as a legitimate strategy.

jokes.text: The dumplings standoff — Michael forbids leftovers, someone offers to take them to a shelter, but Dwight takes his dumplings home to his wife anyway despite Michael's rule
jokes.setup: Michael declares no leftovers as part of maximizing starting weights
jokes.punchline: Dwight defiantly takes his dumplings home to his wife, undermining Michael's absurd authority — and Michael ultimately lets him
jokes.explanation: Functional bit showing the chaotic office dynamic. The shelter mention is a nice dark beat. Dwight's defiance and Michael's capitulation is well-observed but not particularly sharp writing.

jokes.text: Don't go breaking my scale.
jokes.setup: Overweight office employees are lining up to weigh in
jokes.punchline: Michael delivers a casual fat-shaming quip as if it's an administrative instruction
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and perfectly delivered as a throwaway. Michael's casual cruelty is the joke. Economy is excellent — four words do a lot. Slightly cheap but tonally consistent.

jokes.text: Dwight talking-head: 'I'm excited to lose weight for the wedding, because I really want to have washboard abs the first time Angela sees me naked.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is participating in the weight loss contest
jokes.punchline: The reveal that he and Angela — who are secretly engaged — have never seen each other naked, played completely straight by Dwight as romantic aspiration
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The comedy operates on multiple levels: Dwight's earnestness about wanting washboard abs for his secret fiancée, the revelation of their chaste relationship, and the absurd specificity of framing it as motivation for the contest. Only Dwight would say this. The structure is perfect — it starts as a normal motivation and the punchline reframes everything. Justifies 8+ because it's surprising, character-specific, and reveals something about their relationship in one perfectly economical line.

jokes.text: 'Ex-squeeze me.' / 'No, I will ex-squeeze you.'
jokes.setup: Someone says 'ex-squeeze me' (excuse me) as a malapropism
jokes.punchline: The other immediately one-ups it with 'No, I will ex-squeeze you' — a nonsensical but committed escalation
jokes.explanation: A quick wordplay exchange that works because of the immediate confident escalation. The humor is in the complete nonsense of 'I will ex-squeeze you' delivered without irony. Not deep, but economical and fun.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Wait a minute. One more bite of éclair each. Hold it in your mouth if you can't swallow.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to maximize starting weights before the weigh-in
jokes.punchline: He insists on one more bite of éclair, with the instruction to hold it in their mouth if they can't swallow — a completely deranged weight-gaming strategy
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Michael's backwards logic — holding food in your mouth so you weigh more — is wonderfully absurd. The deadpan delivery of 'hold it in your mouth if you can't swallow' is the perfect escalating beat.

jokes.text: The office collectively weighs 2,336 pounds — reaction beat where this number lands on everyone
jokes.setup: The entire office steps on the scale together
jokes.punchline: 2,336 pounds — the sheer number lands as a visual/numerical shock, followed by Michael's 'You all need to learn some portion control'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specific number and Michael's immediate non-sequitur about portion control. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Michael kicks Pam off the scale: 'Pam-cake, no, no, no. We would love your extra poundage, but you are going to be leaving us next week, so vamoose!'
jokes.setup: The office is trying to maximize starting weight — Pam is on the scale
jokes.punchline: Michael would 'love her extra poundage' but kicks her off because she's leaving — the logic being Pam's weight can't help them lose the contest later
jokes.explanation: 'Pam-cake' is a characteristically Michael nickname, and the backwards logic of valuing her 'extra poundage' is consistent with his scheme. The vamoose dismissal lands well. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Kevin asks Pam if she weighs 226 pounds. Holly awkwardly tries to cover. 'Math is hard.' 'Yeah.' 'Just... We'll, just keep going.'
jokes.setup: The group weigh-in shows 2,210 without Pam — Kevin does the subtraction out loud
jokes.punchline: Kevin announces Pam weighs 226 pounds; Holly tries to smooth it over with 'Math is hard' — an awkward, failed save that makes it worse
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured cringe sequence. Kevin's social obliviousness, Holly's well-intentioned but catastrophic save ('Math is hard' — which is itself condescending), and the defeated 'Yeah. Just keep going' aftermath. Each beat escalates the discomfort. Strong character integration: Kevin's inability to read social cues and Holly's HR instinct to smooth things over both fire perfectly. Justifies high score — the 'Math is hard' line is a quotable gem that captures Holly's endearing awkwardness.

jokes.text: Stanley leaves right before weigh-in, claiming he forgot something in his car — clearly sneaking food
jokes.setup: Everyone is competing to lose the most weight; coworkers brag about starvation diets
jokes.punchline: Stanley abruptly exits with a transparently false excuse — the audience knows exactly what he's doing
jokes.explanation: Pure character comedy. Stanley's absolute refusal to participate in anything that inconveniences him is perfectly executed in this one beat. No dialogue needed — the transparent lie is funnier than any explanation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Stanley talking-head: 'I happen to be losing weight on my own for my own reasons.'
jokes.setup: Stanley has just suspiciously left before the weigh-in
jokes.punchline: His defensive, over-explained denial — the double 'own' is the tell — implies he's absolutely not losing weight
jokes.explanation: One of the most economical jokes in the episode. The repetition of 'own' ('on my own for my own reasons') is Stanley's tell — the protest is too emphatic. Perfect deadpan delivery implied, and it lands as both a character beat and a structural joke about what he's NOT saying.

jokes.text: Stanley talking-head with old photo: 'Here's what I used to look like. Look at those biceps. We were fighting the power and eating whatever we wanted.'
jokes.setup: Stanley claims he's losing weight for his own reasons; shows an old photo of himself
jokes.punchline: 'We were fighting the power and eating whatever we wanted' — the juxtaposition of political activism and dietary freedom is absurd and perfect
jokes.explanation: 'Eating whatever we wanted' being listed alongside 'fighting the power' as co-equal life goals is a brilliant character moment. It's unexpected, deeply specific to Stanley, and the photo visual gag supports it. The line is quotable and reveals character depth — Stanley is a man whose rebellious spirit has fully manifested as dietary indulgence.

jokes.text: Andy bursts out: 'Did you see Holly's butt?' Jim: 'No, I didn't. You know why? Because most of the time, friends don't talk about other friends' butts.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Jim are discussing Holly; Andy is excited about her
jokes.punchline: Jim's straight-man lecture about not discussing friends' butts — prim, self-righteous, and slightly absurd in its specificity
jokes.explanation: Jim's prissy correction is funny in its earnestness. 'Most of the time' is a nice hedge that implies there are appropriate times to discuss friends' butts. Solid character work.

jokes.text: Jim lists Holly's qualities: broke her left leg twice in one year, allergic to sesame seeds, read Lonesome Dove three times — then: 'And that her butt refuses to quit.'
jokes.setup: Jim defends himself by listing everything he knows about Holly — all wholesome details
jokes.punchline: 'And that her butt refuses to quit' — the callback to Andy's butt comment, after Jim's righteous deflection, reveals Jim has been thinking about it too
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Jim builds moral authority with three specific, oddly precise details (broke left leg TWICE in one year; Lonesome Dove three times) — then completely undermines himself with the same thing he lectured Andy about. 'Refuses to quit' is a genuinely funny phrase. The misdirection is well-earned, and the callback lands hard. The specificity of the setup details makes the punchline land harder. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: 'That's insane. I thought you had to pee.' — reaction to Jim apparently deciding to wait rather than use the bathroom (following Michael's no-bathroom rule)
jokes.setup: Michael banned bathroom use before weigh-in to keep weights high
jokes.punchline: Jim is actually following the rule — the absurdity of Michael's policy lands when a sensible character complies with it
jokes.explanation: A callback to the no-bathroom rule. The laugh is in Jim complying with an absurd instruction. Functional but not especially sharp.

jokes.text: Holly suggests a yoga teacher as a romantic prospect for a coworker — 'He's a catch.' The coworker responds: 'Actually, I'm a lesbian.' Then immediately walks it back.
jokes.setup: Holly tries to set up a coworker with a man
jokes.punchline: Oscar reflexively claims to be a lesbian, then has to awkwardly un-claim it while explaining his actual reasoning
jokes.explanation: Clever joke using Oscar's established character (gay man). His fumbled attempt to deflect the matchmaking — saying 'I'm a lesbian' when he's a gay man — and the flustered explanation reveals Holly's first day naivety. Holly's genuine confusion ('You think it's a choice?') adds another layer. Good construction.

jokes.text: Holly: 'I'm messing with you, Holly.' — Oscar catches her, and she immediately claims she knew: 'I knew that. Okay, bye.'
jokes.setup: Oscar reveals he was joking about being a lesbian
jokes.punchline: Holly claims she knew but her hasty 'Okay, bye' exit betrays that she absolutely did not
jokes.explanation: The quick exit completing the cringe sequence. Holly's 'I knew that' followed immediately by fleeing is a good beat. Works as a cap on the prior joke.

jokes.text: Pam: 'I will be a little fish in the Big Apple. What up, two-one-two?'
jokes.setup: Pam is excitedly going to New York for an art program
jokes.punchline: 'What up, two-one-two?' — Pam trying on NYC swagger while standing in a Scranton parking lot. Her attempt at cool is charmingly dorky.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Pam. Her excitement translates into a slightly embarrassing attempt at city-person coolness. 'Two-one-two' (NYC area code) is a nice specific touch. Endearing rather than cutting.

jokes.text: Pam is leaving in 10 minutes. Someone asks her to fax something. Jim calls it out; the response: 'It's not going to take her 10 minutes to fax it, Jim.'
jokes.setup: Pam is leaving for New York; Jim is protective of her time
jokes.punchline: The coworker's oblivious literalism — technically correct that faxing takes less than 10 minutes — completely misses the emotional context
jokes.explanation: A quick beat that lands on workplace obliviousness. The straight-faced literalism is the joke. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: 'If I don't see you again, goodbye.' / 'Well, actually, I'll see you when you give me the fax confirmation. So never mind.'
jokes.setup: Coworker attempts a dramatic goodbye to Pam before she leaves for New York
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts it by remembering he'll see her in 30 seconds for the fax confirmation
jokes.explanation: 'So never mind' is a perfect comedic button. The joke is entirely in the structure — the dramatic emotional gesture immediately deflated by practical logistics. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Andy serenades Angela to the tune of 'Umbrella' by Rihanna: 'Ang...ela / Ela, ela, ela / Under my Angerela / Ela, ela, eh, eh'
jokes.setup: Andy is Andy; Angela is nearby
jokes.punchline: Andy adapts 'Umbrella' to 'Angela' — 'Angerela' is a delightfully awkward portmanteau. His earnestness makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: 'Angerela' is a great coinage — it sounds genuinely like a botched musical attempt and captures Andy's can-do obliviousness. Only Andy Bernard would do this. High character integration. The joke has rewatch value because you can hear how hard 'Angerela' tries to work and fails.

jokes.text: Andy pitches The Breakers, Newport, RI as a wedding venue: 'My dad went to Cornell with the current groundskeeper.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants to have his wedding at a grand Newport mansion
jokes.punchline: His connection to the venue is through the groundskeeper — a name-drop that deflates the grandeur immediately
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed joke about Andy's privileged-but-not-quite status. He talks up the mansion and then the connection is the groundskeeper — not even the owner, the GROUNDSKEEPER — via his dad at Cornell. The Cornell drop makes it richer. Very specific, very Andy.

jokes.text: Andy talking-head: 'Every little boy fantasizes about his fairytale wedding.'
jokes.setup: Andy is describing his wedding dreams
jokes.punchline: Delivered as a universal truth — the joke is that it's Andy who says it, with complete sincerity, and the statement itself is a mild gender inversion of the typical trope
jokes.explanation: Seven words doing heavy lifting. It's funny because Andy says it as an obvious truth, while the statement itself is only 'obvious' in Andy's worldview. The sincerity is key — he's not being ironic. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Angela's reactions to Andy's venue pitches: 'No. No.' / 'I don't care. Okay.' / 'How do you feel about Maine?'
jokes.setup: Andy excitedly pitches wedding venues including a sentimental location
jokes.punchline: Angela's utter indifference — 'I don't care. Okay.' — and immediate pivot to Maine is funny because we know she's secretly engaged to someone else
jokes.explanation: The comedy is amplified by dramatic irony — viewers know Angela is secretly engaged to Dwight, making her total disengagement with Andy's wedding plans darkly funny. Her flat 'I don't care. Okay.' is perfectly cold. Rewatch bonus because the irony deepens with knowledge of the Angela-Dwight subplot.

jokes.text: Angela and Dwight's secret romantic moment in the office is followed by: 'Well, that was the last time, Dwight. I mean it.' / 'Monkey.' / 'No. No. I have a fiancé I very much like.'
jokes.setup: Angela is secretly engaged to Andy while still having feelings for Dwight
jokes.punchline: 'I have a fiancé I very much like' — 'very much like' instead of love is a devastating choice of words; delivered by Angela as a firm boundary that reads as self-convincing
jokes.explanation: One of the finest lines in the episode. 'I have a fiancé I very much like' is brilliant in its precise word choice — not love, not love, LIKE — and the 'very much' qualifier makes it both funnier and sadder. Only Angela Martin would use this grammar to describe her romantic partner. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny, it's revealing of her emotional suppression, and it has devastating dramatic irony. Justifies 8+ comfortably — the line is quotable, perfectly constructed, and entirely character-specific. 'Monkey' as Dwight's pet name for Angela is also a perfect standalone beat.

jokes.text: Michael wrote Pam a goodbye poem — the last word is 'seagulls' — and left it upstairs, asking her to wait while he gets it
jokes.setup: Michael wants to give Pam a meaningful send-off
jokes.punchline: The poem is 'really long,' he left it upstairs, and the last word is 'seagulls.' He took 'a lot from other poems.'
jokes.explanation: 'Seagulls' is a perfect comedic word — absurd enough to be funny on its own as a poem's climactic final word. The admission 'I took a lot from other poems' is Michael's casual self-revelation of plagiarism, delivered as an afterthought. The entire sequence (really long, upstairs, last word is seagulls, plagiarized) builds to a perfect character portrait. Highly quotable and deeply Michael.

jokes.text: Jim talking-head: 'Why haven't I proposed yet? ...we just decided that we didn't want to spend the first three months of our engagement apart. Something in her past, I guess. Not really sure of the whole story, but something about a guy who used to work here.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains why he hasn't proposed to Pam yet
jokes.punchline: The show's entire premise — Jim and Pam's will-they-won't-they — is referenced as 'something about a guy who used to work here,' which Jim, the guy, says with apparent lack of self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A masterful piece of meta-comedy. Jim — the guy in question — plays dumb about 'a guy who used to work here' (Roy? himself? both?) while the audience is fully aware. The 'Not really sure of the whole story' is a perfect faux-innocent deflection from a man who IS the story. This is exactly the kind of self-aware joke The Office does exceptionally well. Justifies 8+ — it's structurally elegant, character-perfect, and earns its laugh through wit rather than cheap tricks.

jokes.text: The office lost 31 pounds after week one — genuine celebration erupts
jokes.setup: Everyone has been starving themselves; Michael has been courting Holly
jokes.punchline: Michael's reaction beat — 'I can't believe I'm saying this, but Michael is actually killing it with Holly. And I think I know why. It's because Holly is kind of a major dork.'
jokes.explanation: The talking-head observation that Holly succeeds with Michael because she's 'a major dork' is a nice character insight delivered with affection. Not a huge laugh but a satisfying character beat.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly perform a joint rap: 'I'm MC Mike Scott and I am hot / She's DJ Jazzy Flax and she is the best / All the sucker branches can suck our fat / Wicka-wicka-wicka what?'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are bonding over their shared dorkiness
jokes.punchline: 'All the sucker branches can suck our fat' — an accidental double entendre in a weight-loss context; the entire rap is gloriously bad in a character-authentic way
jokes.explanation: 'Suck our fat' in a weight-loss episode is a perfect accidental joke. The rap is authentically terrible in a way that serves character — Michael fancies himself a performer, Holly is revealed to be equally dorky. 'DJ Jazzy Flax' is a funny name. The whole thing lands because of their genuine enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Jim talking-head about Ronni, the temp: 'I have a feeling I will get to know her very well over the next few years. And eventually declare my love for her.'
jokes.setup: Ronni is filling in for Pam; Jim mentions he doesn't know her
jokes.punchline: Jim deadpans that he will eventually declare his love for her — a pointed self-aware joke about his romantic history with the receptionist
jokes.explanation: Jim's meta-awareness of his own narrative pattern — falling for the receptionist — is executed with perfect deadpan economy. The 'few years' timeline is a great specific detail. This is the show being smart about itself without being smug. Justifies 8+ for its structure, character-specificity, and the way it rewards longtime viewers.

jokes.text: Pam shows up to the wrong class at Pratt, sits down anyway, and the professor calls her out: 'It looks like I'm boring someone already.' / 'No, I just...' / 'Please sit down.'
jokes.setup: Pam accidentally sits in the wrong class at Pratt
jokes.punchline: The professor singles her out before she can explain, and she just... sits down and stays, presumably in the wrong class
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup. Pam's deer-in-headlights response to being called out, then silently complying with staying in the wrong class, is very Pam. The joke would play better visually.

jokes.text: Kelly is shaking and snapping at people on day three of her maple syrup/lemon juice/cayenne pepper cleanse. Talking-head: 'I just bought some bikinis online, size two. So... Gonna look amazing!'
jokes.setup: Kelly is on an extreme cleanse diet
jokes.punchline: Her manic, hollow positivity ('Gonna look amazing!') contrasted with her visible physical deterioration is the joke — the exclamation point is doing enormous work
jokes.explanation: Kelly's character — obsessed with appearance and trends to a dangerous degree — is perfectly captured. The specific ingredients of the cleanse are funny (maple syrup + cayenne + lemon juice), and the juxtaposition with her shaking body and then sunny 'Gonna look amazing!' is a strong comedic contrast. Very Kelly.

jokes.text: Jan shows up at the office to use the copier. 'How's the candle game?' / 'Serenity by Jan is kicking ass and taking names.' / 'You remember last week when that girl went missing — guess whose candles they used for the vigil?' / 'Cool. Thank God they found her, too.' / 'Oh, they found her?'
jokes.setup: Jan is selling candles under her brand 'Serenity by Jan'
jokes.punchline: Jan's proudest marketing case study is a missing child vigil — and she didn't know the child was found. The 'Oh, they found her?' reveals Jan's singular focus on her candle brand over all human concern.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Jan brags about brand exposure (vigil candles), the listener expresses relief the child was found, and Jan's 'Oh, they found her?' reveals she never followed up on the actual human story — she only cared about the candles. The dark implication that Jan's brand awareness required a child to go missing, and that she's almost disappointed the story ended happily (less candle usage?), is brilliantly written. Perfectly structured, deeply character-specific to post-breakdown Jan, quotable, and earned through excellent setup. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Oscar about Jan: 'She's very beautiful.' / 'Yeah, she is. And clinically insane.'
jokes.setup: A new employee notices Jan in Michael's office
jokes.punchline: 'And clinically insane' — delivered with the same casual weight as 'she's beautiful'
jokes.explanation: The economy is excellent — four words conveying years of shared office trauma with Jan. The deadpan delivery is key. Not a deeply original observation but executed with perfect economy.

jokes.text: Oscar, after the lesbian/yoga incident, quietly goes back to Holly: 'I don't know if your offer still stands or whatever, but you can give your yoga teacher my number.'
jokes.setup: Oscar had earlier awkwardly claimed to be a lesbian when Holly tried to set him up
jokes.punchline: Oscar's quiet, sheepish walk-back — 'I don't know if your offer still stands or whatever' — lands as a perfect humiliated callback
jokes.explanation: The 'or whatever' is perfect — Oscar is trying to be casual about something deeply embarrassing. A well-constructed callback that rewards the earlier scene. The understatement of 'I don't know if your offer still stands' is funny in context.

jokes.text: Dwight berates Kevin over the spreadsheet — Holly intervenes, defending him. Then Holly reveals she thinks Kevin is mentally challenged: 'He is mentally challenged. But he's doing a super job here.'
jokes.setup: Holly stands up to Dwight for bullying Kevin
jokes.punchline: Holly thinks she's being supportive — but she genuinely believes Kevin is mentally challenged, which is both horrifying and funny, especially Kevin's confused 'Do you think that I'm retarded?'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's crown jewels. The joke operates through perfect misdirection: Holly appears to be the good HR hero standing up to Dwight's bullying, but her intervention is itself based on a fundamental misunderstanding. 'He's doing a super job here' is the HR-approved condescension of someone who thinks they're being generous. Kevin's devastated 'Do you think that I'm retarded?' is the perfect button — he's outraged, and his outrage is funny because Kevin IS often kind of... slow. The fact that Dwight then calls Holly out for being offensive, when he was the one being cruel, is a perfect irony layer. Multiple levels of comedy, all earned. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Kevin talking-head, crushed: 'Do you think that I'm retarded?'
jokes.setup: Holly has just 'defended' Kevin by confirming she thinks he's mentally challenged
jokes.punchline: Kevin's direct, hurt question to camera — the absurdity is that his umbrage is completely legitimate, but Kevin asking this question is itself funny
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfect delivery. Kevin's wounded dignity is genuinely moving and funny simultaneously. The joke works because Kevin asking this question is simultaneously absurd (given Kevin's demonstrated limitations) and completely valid (Holly had no reason to assume this). The camera-facing delivery amplifies everything. Among the most quotable moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Andy's four non-refundable wedding deposits: 'Hot air balloons over Napa Valley, world famous Walt Disney's Epcot Center, scuba diving wedding in the Bahamas, and Wilkes-Barre Marriott Ballroom C.' Angela's reaction: 'Dangerous, tacky, sharks, haunted. No.'
jokes.setup: Andy has made non-refundable deposits at four venues to accommodate Angela's impossible standards
jokes.punchline: Angela dispatches all four with one-word verdicts — 'Dangerous, tacky, sharks, haunted' — 'haunted' for the Marriott being the unexpected comic peak
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic escalation and economy. The list of venues goes from legitimately grand (Napa hot air balloons, Bahamas) to hilariously mundane (Wilkes-Barre Marriott Ballroom C — not A, not B, C). Angela's rapid-fire one-word rejections are perfect: 'dangerous' and 'sharks' are literal, 'tacky' for Epcot is devastating snobbery, and 'haunted' for the Marriott is a completely unexpected supernatural concern delivered with the same flat authority. The list structure, the comedic escalation to Ballroom C, and Angela's perfectly calibrated one-word responses make this among the best-constructed jokes in the episode. Justifies the high score.

jokes.text: Andy talking-head about his sleep routine: 'I have a nice comforter and several cozy pillows. I usually read a chapter of a book and it's lights-out by 8:30. That's how I sleep at night.'
jokes.setup: The phrase 'that's how I sleep at night' is typically used to justify a moral decision
jokes.punchline: Andy takes it literally — it's a description of his actual bedtime routine, delivered as if it were moral justification
jokes.explanation: A sharp wordplay joke built on literalism. Andy delivers his bedtime routine — comforter, pillows, chapter of a book, lights out by 8:30 — as the punchline to 'that's how I sleep at night.' The 8:30 bedtime is the perfect specific detail. Subverts the idiom elegantly and is very much in Andy's character (earnest, slightly childlike).

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's first video call — Jim is still trying to set it up while Pam riffs: 'Ceramics class, then dinner by myself. I'm going to watch HGTV, and maybe go to Bungalow 8 with John Mayer.'
jokes.setup: Pam is reporting her NYC life; Jim is barely online yet
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of NYC plans climaxes at 'Bungalow 8 with John Mayer' — a celebrity name-drop so absurd it works as a signal that Pam is riffing for fun
jokes.explanation: Pam testing the boundaries of what she can say while Jim is distracted — 'John Mayer' is the obvious joke that shows she's messing with him. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Ronni as 'Rice-a-Ronni': 'She is hilarious, she is wonderful, a beam of light in this dark, dark office.' / Ronni in talking-head: 'Not really so much. All she does is plop herself down there and answer phones all day. The nerve.'
jokes.setup: Michael effusively praises Ronni (Pam's temp replacement) over video call with Pam
jokes.punchline: Ronni's talking-head deflation — 'not really so much' — and the revelation she's annoyed at being praised for basic job functions: 'answer phones all day. The nerve.'
jokes.explanation: 'The nerve' as Ronni's deadpan self-description of answering phones is funny — she's sarcastically modest to the point of being confusing. 'Rice-a-Ronni' is also a good Michael nickname (his affinity for food-based nicknames).

jokes.text: Michael's 'real beef' with Ronni: she can't find the colored paperclips. He asks Pam — via video call from New York — to help Ronni find them on the supply shelf.
jokes.setup: Michael is video calling Pam in New York
jokes.punchline: Michael asks Pam — who is in New York — to walk Ronni to the supply shelf via webcam to find paperclips. The webcam follows Ronni to the supply shelf.
jokes.explanation: The visual of the entire office following a laptop showing Pam's face to the supply shelf is wonderfully absurd. Michael's inability to just tell Ronni where the paperclips are — he has to involve Pam from New York — is a perfect character beat. The physical comedy of the procession adds to it.

jokes.text: After week two weigh-in: 'You all gained five pounds back. Damn it. Come on!'
jokes.setup: The office celebrated losing 31 pounds the previous week
jokes.punchline: They gained five back — the running gag of the office's inability to lose weight lands as a satisfying beat
jokes.explanation: Functional payoff to the weight-loss contest running gag. Not sharp writing — the joke is just the predictable failure. Works as a structural beat.

jokes.text: One branch lost a pound — because a character was hospitalized on an IV for two days: 'I lost four pounds.' / 'I don't know what those other fools were doing, but I lost four pounds.'
jokes.setup: Branches are competing to lose weight
jokes.punchline: Hospitalisation as a diet strategy — proudly claimed with total conviction. The dismissal of 'those other fools' elevates it.
jokes.explanation: Dark joke about hospitalisation as weight-loss win. The confidence is the joke. 'Those other fools' is a funny touch — implying others should have been better at getting hospitalised.

jokes.text: Phyllis has replaced Angela on the Party Planning Committee. 'I guess I was just in the right place at the right time.'
jokes.setup: Angela has been deposed from the Party Planning Committee
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's false modesty — 'right place at the right time' — for what is clearly an office power play
jokes.explanation: Phyllis's smug false modesty about a committee coup is perfectly delivered. Works as a character beat that pays off their long-running power dynamic.

jokes.text: Phyllis suggests fruit instead of cake for the birthday party. Michael: 'We only lost one pound, Phyllis.'
jokes.setup: The office is on a weight loss competition; Phyllis proposes healthy party food
jokes.punchline: Michael — who has been pushing weight loss — immediately rejects healthy food as insufficient reward for losing a single pound. His internal logic is exposed.
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-defeating logic is the joke — he's undermining his own contest. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael talking-head: 'They have no willpower. I once went 28 years without having sex. And then again for seven years.'
jokes.setup: Michael is complaining about the office's lack of willpower for the weight loss contest
jokes.punchline: His example of willpower — going 28 years without sex, then seven more — is a devastating self-own delivered without any awareness
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect Michael Scott joke. The structure is elegant: he's lecturing others about willpower, then reveals his example of willpower is involuntary celibacy — which he has somehow repeated. The 'and then again for seven years' escalation is what makes it great; the second beat implies the first time wasn't just bad luck. He's completely unaware this makes him sound pathetic. This is close to the 'snip snap' anchor example in quality — a devastating character self-reveal delivered as boasting. Easily justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'Does anyone have any idea what the number one cause of death is in this country?' / 'Shotgun weddings.' / 'That's not what that is.' / 'Fright. Being scared to death.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks a rhetorical question about death statistics
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Shotgun weddings' and Kevin's 'Fright. Being scared to death.' as sincere answers — neither has any idea what a shotgun wedding is or basic health statistics
jokes.explanation: 'Shotgun weddings' is funny because Andy clearly has no idea what the term means and is guessing based on 'death' + 'weddings'. 'Fright. Being scared to death.' is Kevin at peak Kevin — he's parsed the word 'death' and worked backwards. Two separate wrong answers that are character-perfect for their speakers.

jokes.text: 'I want us all to live forever. How? How are we going to do this?' / 'Cryogenics.' / 'Beer me five.'
jokes.setup: Michael wants the office to be healthy and live forever
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'Cryogenics' is a serious answer; 'Beer me five' is Michael's slang for 'gimme five' delivered in response to the cryogenics plan
jokes.explanation: Dwight suggesting cryogenics with total seriousness is on-brand. 'Beer me five' as Michael's slang for a high-five is a nice characterization detail — he would absolutely say this.

jokes.text: Jan stops Jim: 'I don't want you to end up with a surprise pregnancy like me.' Hands him condoms.
jokes.setup: Jim is heading out to see Pam in New York
jokes.punchline: Jan — Michael's unstable ex — spontaneously counsels Jim about contraception and hands him condoms, framing her own pregnancy as a cautionary tale
jokes.explanation: Only Jan would do this. The phrase 'surprise pregnancy like me' implies her own pregnancy is a tragedy she's warning others about, while her baby is right there in the office. The casual intimacy of handing condoms to a coworker's boyfriend is perfectly Jan-level inappropriate. Jim's 'Okay. Thank you for this.' response is the appropriate deadpan.

jokes.text: Angela's impossible wedding requirements list: 'Thousand-year-old church in the continental United States. There has to be a rainbow. 24-hour veterinarian on call.'
jokes.setup: Angela has impossible standards for the wedding venue
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from merely difficult (thousand-year-old church — which doesn't exist in the US) to magical thinking (rainbow) to practical absurdity (24-hour vet)
jokes.explanation: The escalating list is excellent writing. A thousand-year-old US church is geographically impossible (the US isn't that old) — which means Angela's standards are literally impossible from item one. The rainbow requirement is magical thinking. The 24-hour vet is Angela prioritizing her cats' access to medical care over the wedding venue. All three are deeply, specifically Angela Martin. 'That is very important to me' makes it funnier. Justifies high score — the joke is structurally tight and utterly character-specific.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I'll marry you right here in this building. I'll marry you in the parking lot. I'll marry you in the eye of a hurricane in the middle of a snow storm on top of a monsoon.'
jokes.setup: Jim wants to reassure Pam he doesn't care about the venue
jokes.punchline: 'In the eye of a hurricane in the middle of a snow storm on top of a monsoon' — the meteorological escalation collapses into absurdity, three disaster events simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Sweet romantic moment with a comedic turn — 'on top of a monsoon' is the absurdist escalation that tips it into comedy while keeping the sincerity. The triple weather disaster is a nice structural gag.

jokes.text: Michael shows off Pam's art (which we can see is a building sketch) to Holly: 'Oh. So rude of me. Have you seen Pam's new art? It's right there. Check it out.' — a long silence as Holly looks at it.
jokes.setup: Michael wants to show Holly something impressive
jokes.punchline: The long beat as Holly looks at Pam's art — the implication being the art is not impressive, and the silence communicates everything
jokes.explanation: A visual/silence beat that works primarily in watching the episode. The pause while Holly considers how to respond to mediocre art is a classic Office awkward silence. Less effective in transcript form.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head from Pam's dorm: 'Some girl came into Pam's room crying about her roommate stealing her soy milk. So I'm in here waiting it out.'
jokes.setup: Jim has visited Pam at her New York dorm
jokes.punchline: Jim hiding in Pam's room to avoid college-student drama about soy milk — his deadpan delivery frames this as a reasonable tactical decision
jokes.explanation: A nice observational joke about the age gap between Jim (mid-20s professional) and Pam's Pratt classmates (early 20s art students). 'Waiting it out' as a tactical response to soy milk drama is characteristically Jim. Good economy.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Stanley, you can eat a slice of your birthday cake.' Stanley: 'I don't like cake anymore.' / 'Why not, dawg?' / 'Taste changed. Now all I like is baklava.'
jokes.setup: Stanley is known for loving cake; Michael offers him some at his birthday party
jokes.punchline: Stanley now exclusively likes baklava — his tastes have completely changed and he states this without explanation or apology
jokes.explanation: Stanley's pivot to baklava is delivered with perfect finality — no explanation offered or needed. 'Taste changed' as a complete sentence is great. Michael's 'Why not, dawg?' is also a funny beat. The specificity of baklava (not just 'other sweets') is what makes this work — it's a very particular and arbitrary new preference.

jokes.text: Michael: 'We should have a party and not invite them.' / 'Yeah. Let's go mini-golfing.' / 'Yeah?' / Holly: 'Oh, hey, could I have a rain check on the mini-golf? I actually have a date tonight.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to hang out with Holly and the group
jokes.punchline: Holly has a date — Michael's visible disappointment, implied but not stated, is the cringe beat; the 'rain check on mini-golf' phrasing is delightfully mundane
jokes.explanation: Setup for Michael's romantic disappointment. The comedy here is mostly in what's not said — Michael's reaction to Holly's date. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael about Holly's date prospects: 'I think you'll have fun because men from Scranton are handsome and they know how to show a woman a good time. Not that guy who murdered his mother. He was not so handsome. Also Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to hype up Holly's dating prospects in Scranton
jokes.punchline: He immediately self-corrects for a mother-murderer, then casually adds 'Also Kevin' as an exception — implying Kevin is in the same category of disqualified prospects, though for very different reasons
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. Michael is trying to be supportive, then carves out the mother-murderer exception (dark and specific), then adds 'Also Kevin' — which conflates Kevin with a murderer while presumably meaning something much more benign (Kevin is unattractive/awkward). The comma-level pause between 'Also Kevin' and the previous statement is what makes it devastating. This is Michael at his best — accidentally insulting everyone in the process of trying to be helpful. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Holly doesn't need luck. Everyone that meets her instantly loves her.' Then immediately: 'Party's over! You're so busted!'
jokes.setup: Michael has just had a sweet moment endorsing Holly
jokes.punchline: His sentiment is immediately interrupted by him catching the office eating cake — the whiplash from sincere to disciplinarian is a good tonal contrast
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition works but is fairly predictable. A standard Michael pivot from sentiment to authority.

jokes.text: Michael's talking-head spin: 'The bad news is we're not doing very well, so we really had to starve ourselves this whole week. But the good news is all the other branches are doing just as bad as we are... So if we stay fat long enough, we may actually get a whole month off.'
jokes.setup: The prize has been upped to five days because all branches are failing
jokes.punchline: 'If we stay fat long enough, we may actually get a whole month off' — Michael reframes catastrophic failure as a strategic opportunity
jokes.explanation: Excellent Michael logic that is actually internally coherent — if the prize keeps increasing as everyone fails, staying fat IS strategically sound. The absurdity is that he's right. 'If we stay fat long enough' is a great quotable line. Strong character integration — Michael always finds the silver lining through creative self-delusion.

jokes.text: Dwight talking-head: 'I swallowed a tapeworm last night. It's going to grow up to three feet inside of me and then it eats all my food so that I don't get fat. And then after three months, I take some medicine and then I pass it.' / 'Creed sold it to me. It's from Mexico.'
jokes.setup: The weight loss contest; Dwight is highly competitive
jokes.punchline: Dwight has intentionally swallowed a tapeworm purchased from Creed, from Mexico — each detail escalates the horror. 'Creed sold it to me' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: One of the all-time great Office jokes. Every element is perfect: Dwight's complete comfort with parasitic infection as a diet strategy, the clinical description ('grows to three feet,' 'I pass it'), and the devastating final detail — 'Creed sold it to me. It's from Mexico.' Creed as the office's black market tapeworm supplier is so specific and so correct. The joke earns its dark comedy through sheer commitment and character logic — of course Dwight would do this, of course Creed sells tapeworms. This is near-'snip snap' territory. The response beat from Creed ('That wasn't a tapeworm') is the perfect button that adds another layer of horror. Justifies the high score emphatically.

jokes.text: Creed's talking-head response to the tapeworm revelation: 'That wasn't a tapeworm.'
jokes.setup: Dwight reveals Creed sold him a tapeworm
jokes.punchline: Creed's flat denial/correction — we don't know what he actually sold Dwight, and not knowing is worse
jokes.explanation: Four words that are among the best in the episode. The joke is entirely what's unsaid: if it wasn't a tapeworm, what was it? Creed's delivery of this as a flat correction — not alarm, not explanation, just a quiet clarification — is perfect comedy. It's more disturbing than anything Dwight could have said because it implies Creed has a taxonomy of things he sells that are worse than tapeworms. Economy is a perfect 10 — you cannot improve this joke by adding a single word. Character integration is absolute — no one else on television could deliver this line. One of the finest joke-cap moments in The Office's run.

jokes.text: Ryan returns with a goatee. Jim: 'And you got a goatee.' Ryan: 'I did.' Jim: 'Did you get that after you helped me move and you saw mine?' Ryan: 'Yes.' Jim: 'Goatee!' / 'Fired guy!'
jokes.setup: Ryan has returned from his fall from grace; he's trying to reconnect
jokes.punchline: Kevin greeting Ryan as 'Fired guy!' — puncturing Ryan's attempt at a smooth return; Kevin's cheerful tactlessness is the joke
jokes.explanation: The goatee bit between Jim and Ryan (Ryan copying Jim's goatee is a quiet character humiliation) is well-played. Kevin's 'Fired guy!' arrival is perfectly Kevin — warm, enthusiastic, and devastating. The goatee exchange establishes how far Ryan has fallen (imitating Jim) before Kevin hammers it home.

jokes.text: Ryan's apology to Jim includes: 'I realized there's so much more to life than being the youngest VP in the company's history.' Jim: 'You're talking about your court-ordered community service?' Ryan: 'I don't need a judge to tell me to keep my community clean.' Jim: 'But he did, right?'
jokes.setup: Ryan is performing a sincere redemption arc speech to Jim
jokes.punchline: Jim punctures Ryan's spiritual awakening by identifying it as legally mandated; Ryan's defense ('I don't need a judge to tell me') is itself deflated by 'But he did, right?'
jokes.explanation: 'But he did, right?' is a perfect Jim Halpert line — flat, persistent, completely deflating. The structure is excellent: Ryan's speech, Jim's diagnosis, Ryan's defense, Jim's final press. Four beats, perfectly calibrated. Jim refusing to let Ryan escape into inspiration-speak is satisfying character comedy. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Kelly and I are the only ones who've either passed out or almost passed out!'
jokes.setup: Michael is frustrated no one is trying hard enough to lose weight
jokes.punchline: His standard for commitment is fainting — and he's proud to be in the 'passed out' category alongside Kelly as a measure of dedication
jokes.explanation: Michael measuring effort by near-medical emergencies is a good character beat. 'Either passed out or almost passed out' as a two-tier achievement system is funny in its specificity.

jokes.text: Michael talking-head: 'This is the hardest thing I've ever had to do in my entire life. I haven't had a very hard life.'
jokes.setup: Michael says the weight loss contest is the hardest thing he's ever done
jokes.punchline: The immediate self-aware qualifier: 'I haven't had a very hard life' — which contextualizes everything and makes the first statement funnier
jokes.explanation: An exceptional two-sentence joke. The structure is near-perfect: extreme claim ('hardest thing I've ever done') immediately undercut by a disarming confession of privilege ('I haven't had a very hard life'). This is Michael Scott at his most self-aware while still being self-unaware — he says it as if it helps explain things, not realizing it makes him sound even more pathetic. Highly quotable and applicable. Economy is almost perfect. Justifies 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Dwight confronting Michael about Holly's date: 'This is your fault. No. Your stupid friend zone. I should have been lovers with her first and then friends. That was terrible advice. Terrible advice! You know my seduction method. I like to get in there and get my hands dirty. You sabotaged me. You sabotaged me, man!'
jokes.setup: Holly has a date with someone else; Dwight had advised Michael to be her friend first
jokes.punchline: Dwight's seduction philosophy — 'get in there and get my hands dirty' — and his conviction that Michael was 'sabotaged' through friendship is pure Dwight worldview
jokes.explanation: 'I like to get in there and get my hands dirty' as a description of Dwight's romantic methodology is perfectly disturbing. His conviction that 'friends first' is a sabotage strategy reveals his purely transactional view of relationships. The repetition of 'you sabotaged me' is funny in its escalating outrage.

jokes.text: Michael's liposuction proposal: 'I'm going to randomly select three names and these three people will get liposuction.' / 'Stanley, Phyllis, Kevin. And you will be responsible for your own medical bills.'
jokes.setup: The office is struggling to lose weight with weeks left in the contest
jokes.punchline: Michael proposes mandatory liposuction for randomly selected employees — who must pay for it themselves. The randomness that immediately produces the three largest employees is also a joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'random' selection of exactly Stanley, Phyllis, and Kevin — the office's heaviest employees — is a perfect joke within a joke. The employees-pay-for-their-own-mandatory-medical-procedures kicker is classically Michael: generous impulse, zero follow-through on the generosity.

jokes.text: Ryan apologizes to Kelly: 'I think I never really processed 9/11.' Kelly's response: 'Cool. We should get a drink later, catch up.' / 'Pick me up around 8:00?'
jokes.setup: Ryan is doing a formal apology tour; Kelly is his ex
jokes.punchline: Ryan's invoking 9/11 as an excuse for treating Kelly badly is astounding in its self-serving absurdity. Kelly's immediate 'Cool' and pivot to planning a date is equally absurd — she accepts this completely.
jokes.explanation: 'I think I never really processed 9/11' as Ryan's explanation for treating Kelly badly — when Ryan was a college student during 9/11 and this has nothing to do with anything — is a masterpiece of self-serving millennial excuse-making. And Kelly's completely unquestioning acceptance ('Cool') followed by immediately setting a date is perfect Kelly: she doesn't care about the reasoning, she just wants Ryan back. Both characters are simultaneously at their worst and most themselves. This is exceptional character writing. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Kelly's brutal rejection of Ryan's reconciliation attempt: 'I'm dating Darryl still and we're like crazy in love, so...' / Ryan: 'Cool.' — five-second pause — 'Well, maybe I'll see you around. It's a small office.'
jokes.setup: Ryan has done his apology and charm offensive; Kelly seemed receptive
jokes.punchline: Kelly has a new relationship and is blissfully unaware of how devastating this is to Ryan, whose humiliation plays out in the pause before his pathetic 'Well, maybe I'll see you around'
jokes.explanation: 'It's a small office' after being utterly rejected in that office is a perfect piece of deflated dialogue. Ryan's 'Cool' (mirroring Kelly's 'Cool' from his apology, now landing with different weight) and the pause before 'Well, maybe I'll see you around' is beautifully cringe. The awkward silence beat between the rejection and his response is the heart of the joke.

jokes.text: Jim is hiding from his ex-girlfriend in a restaurant: 'Just hide me.' / 'Wow, was it the age difference?' / 'Actually, kind of, yes. I just didn't like eating dinner that early.'
jokes.setup: Jim sees an ex-girlfriend at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: The age gap is confirmed by the punchline — he dated someone old enough that dinner was at an early-bird special time. The specificity of 'eating dinner that early' as the dealbreaker is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully efficient. The age-gap joke is delivered entirely through the indirect implication of early-bird dinner — never explicitly stating the woman was old, just giving one very specific symptom. This is how The Office does its best jokes: through implication and specificity rather than stating the joke directly.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head from the restaurant: 'I made friends.' — as a triumphant conclusion to hiding from his ex-girlfriend
jokes.setup: Jim was hiding from his ex; context of the scene
jokes.punchline: 'I made friends' as the triumphant conclusion — the bar is so low, and Jim delivers it with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Three words. 'I made friends' as self-congratulation for surviving an awkward encounter. The economy is perfect — it implies the whole scene (hiding, eventual contact, the social success) in three words. Satisfying micro-joke.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals there was no client — he drove Phyllis to an abandoned warehouse five miles away and pushed her out of the car. She had to walk home with no money and no phone.
jokes.setup: Dwight proposed a sales call partnership with Phyllis
jokes.punchline: The 'client meeting' was Dwight's weight-loss scheme — he stranded Phyllis to make her walk for exercise
jokes.explanation: An excellent dark reveal. Dwight's resourcefulness in finding extreme weight-loss solutions (tapeworm, now stranding Phyllis) is consistent and hilarious. The callback to their deal — 60-40 split, Phyllis drives — now reads as Phyllis unknowingly agreeing to be his fitness hostage. 'I took your purse. What are you worried about?' is the perfect Dwight defense.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Phyllis Vance, ladies and gentlemen.' — applauding Phyllis being stranded and forced to walk, as a weight loss achievement
jokes.setup: Phyllis has just reported being abandoned at an abandoned warehouse
jokes.punchline: Michael celebrates the forced exercise as a win for the weight loss contest
jokes.explanation: Michael's endorsement of Dwight's abduction as a wellness strategy is a good dark beat. Less sharp as a standalone joke but works as a character response.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I took your purse. What are you worried about?'
jokes.setup: Phyllis protests being abandoned in a bad part of town with no money or phone
jokes.punchline: Dwight's logic: he took her purse (so she wasn't robbed), therefore the situation was safe. This is presented as complete reassurance.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely brilliant Dwight joke. His logic is internally consistent (no purse = no mugging target) while being completely insane (stranding someone without money is itself the problem). The question mark turns a monstrous act into a sincere inquiry about her concern. Only Dwight. Economy is near-perfect. Justifies high score — this is among the episode's best individual lines.

jokes.text: Phyllis calls David Wallace: 'Dunder Mifflin wants to make it clear that Dunder Mifflin does not discriminate nor does it condone unhealthy dieting habits or extreme weight loss strategies, as was clearly stated in the official...' — Michael interrupts: 'Oh, bang, boom, shake, klump!'
jokes.setup: Phyllis is filing a complaint to corporate about being abandoned
jokes.punchline: Michael bursts in with 'Oh, bang, boom, shake, klump!' — his entrance as Michael Klump, his fat suit character, at the exact moment corporate is being informed of his abuses
jokes.explanation: The comic timing — Phyllis reading the corporate disclaimer while Michael charges in as his fat character — is well-structured. 'Bang, boom, shake, klump' as Michael's entrance fanfare is characteristically absurd.

jokes.text: Michael enters in a half-inflated sumo suit as 'Michael Klump.' Holly calls it out: 'Because you're kind of doing Michael Klump.' / 'How do you know Michael Klump?' / 'Because it's your making fun of fat people character.' / 'How dare you! Michael Klump is a celebration of fat people.'
jokes.setup: Michael arrives in a sumo suit to give a body image presentation
jokes.punchline: Holly immediately identifies and names the character; Michael's outraged denial that Klump is 'a celebration' rather than mockery; Holly's 'I think of him as more like a monster'
jokes.explanation: Holly's outsider perspective on the office's normalized insanity is the engine of her character comedy, and it fires here. She names what Michael's character is ('making fun of fat people') with HR precision, and Michael's genuine offense ('How dare you! Michael Klump is a CELEBRATION') is exactly the self-deception that defines him. 'I think of him as more like a monster' as Holly's cool professional assessment is perfect. Justifies high score.

jokes.text: Holly and Michael debate whether 'I say, I say, I say, I'll sit on you' is Klump's catchphrase. Michael corrects her wrong version while demonstrating his own 'correct' version of the same thing.
jokes.setup: Michael insists Michael Klump is a celebration; Holly quotes his 'I'll sit on you' catchphrase
jokes.punchline: Michael corrects her technically-correct version of the offensive catchphrase — the distinction he's drawing is meaningless, but he draws it seriously
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Michael's fierce ownership of the precise wording of his offensive character's catchphrase. His dignity is fully invested in the correct delivery of 'I say, I say, I say, I'll sit on you.' Solid continuation of the Klump sequence.

jokes.text: Holly confronts Michael: 'Because you're kind of doing Michael Klump.' Michael: 'How do you know Michael Klump?' Holly: 'Because it's your making-fun-of-fat-people character.' Michael: 'How dare you! Michael Klump is a celebration of fat people.' Holly: 'I think of him as more like a monster.'
jokes.setup: Michael is in a fat suit claiming to be doing a body-positive presentation
jokes.punchline: Holly sees through the 'celebration' framing immediately — 'I think of him as more like a monster' — and Michael's outrage at having his offensive character correctly characterized is the cringe pivot
jokes.explanation: Holly's accurate read of Michael — delivered with specific detail ('making-fun-of-fat-people character') — establishes her as smart enough to cut through his rationalizations. 'I think of him as more like a monster' is a good dry line.

jokes.text: Michael's body image speech about the building: 'Look at the outside of this building. It is ugly. But you come inside and it is beautiful. Just like this unappealing fat suit. Inside is a rather handsome, sexy man.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to give a body image lesson
jokes.punchline: The extended metaphor about the ugly building collapses into Michael complimenting himself — 'a rather handsome, sexy man' — as if this is the lesson's moral
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'lesson about body image' becoming a compliment to himself is perfectly predictable in the best way — the joke is that he can't help it. 'Rather handsome, sexy man' is a nice self-assessment.

jokes.text: Dwight is asked to apologize to Phyllis for the abandoned-warehouse incident. His apology: 'I apologize for creating a ruse which forced you to exercise.' Michael: 'Finally. Right?' Michael then compliments Phyllis's 'gams.'
jokes.setup: Dwight must apologize to Phyllis
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'apology' is entirely framed around the outcome (exercise) with no acknowledgment of the harm — and Michael accepts it as a real apology, then immediately ogles Phyllis's legs
jokes.explanation: 'I apologize for creating a ruse which forced you to exercise' is a perfect non-apology apology — Dwight frames the harm (ruse, abandonment, taking her purse) entirely as 'exercise creation.' The legalistic framing is on-brand. Michael's 'gams' comment as his version of celebrating Phyllis lands as a secondary cringe beat.

jokes.text: Dwight's apology: 'I apologize for creating a ruse which forced you to exercise.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is being compelled to apologize to Phyllis for abandoning her miles from the office
jokes.punchline: His apology uses corporate/legal language ('creating a ruse') to describe a mildly criminal act — and characterizes forced exercise as the offense rather than the abandonment, theft, and deception
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'creating a ruse which forced you to exercise' is exceptional — it's both a precise bureaucratic construction and a complete moral failure. Dwight's distillation of kidnapping-adjacent behavior into 'exercise facilitation' is perfect character comedy. 'Which forced you to exercise' as the key offense (not the theft, not the abandonment) shows his values perfectly.

jokes.text: Michael puts Kelly on a chair so the office can name her beautiful features. Andy: 'Hell of an ass.' Kevin: 'I wonder what people like about me.' / Meredith: 'Probably my jugs.'
jokes.setup: Michael's body image exercise: stand Kelly on a chair, list beautiful things about her
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Hell of an ass' as a sincere answer to 'What makes her beautiful?' Kevin's immediate pivot to what people like about HIM, and Meredith's self-assessment of 'my jugs'
jokes.explanation: Three separate character-perfect responses in quick succession. Andy's earnest objectification ('Hell of an ass' said with complete sincerity as a compliment), Kevin's narcissistic pivot, and Meredith's completely unfiltered self-assessment all land as character comedy. 'Probably my jugs' is a very Meredith line.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head from summer: 'Summer's going great. Just spent two hours listening to Michael Klump. I have a weird pain in my left side that I'm convinced is an ulcer. My girlfriend lives in New York, and I haven't seen her in 10 days. How's your summer?'
jokes.setup: Jim has just endured Michael's Klump presentation
jokes.punchline: The relentless deadpan accumulation of miseries delivered as a casual check-in, culminating in 'How's your summer?' turned on the viewer
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed talking-head. The list of genuine miseries (two hours of Klump, potential ulcer, long-distance girlfriend) delivered with complete equanimity, then 'How's your summer?' flipping the camera relationship — Jim addressing the audience directly — is a signature Jim Halpert moment. The left-side pain 'I'm convinced is an ulcer' is a great specific detail. Justifies high score for its structure, the payoff flip, and the character-perfect delivery.

jokes.text: Holly's date was an 8.5 but she got a red wine stain on her favorite shirt. Three days later, no call. She has Counting Crows tickets for tonight.
jokes.setup: Holly's date went well; now she's waiting for him to call
jokes.punchline: The 8.5 rating of a date where she stained her shirt is mildly funny; the Counting Crows tickets add tragicomic pathos to the waiting
jokes.explanation: The Counting Crows detail is the most specific and funny element — it's a very 2008 choice of concert to have tickets for. The 8.5 rating with a shirt stain is mildly amusing. Mostly setup for later beats.

jokes.text: 'I say we have a parade.' — in response to the office losing 4 pounds
jokes.setup: The office lost four pounds
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately proposes a parade — the disproportionate celebration is the joke
jokes.explanation: Short and character-appropriate. Michael's impulse to celebrate with maximum festivity regardless of the accomplishment scale is a running character trait. Not especially crafted but snappy.

jokes.text: Andy talks-head about his nephew's tee ball game: 'Tonight is my nephew's tee ball game and I kind of missed the first three, so...' Pam: 'You've already disappointed him so much. He can't be expecting a lot from you.' Andy: 'I know. I suck.' Pam: 'Yes, you do.'
jokes.setup: Andy is considering skipping his nephew's tee ball game
jokes.punchline: Pam's completely unfiltered assessment — 'You've already disappointed him so much, he can't be expecting a lot' — is shockingly honest, and Andy's resigned 'I know. I suck' followed by Pam's 'Yes, you do' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Pam's 'he can't be expecting a lot from you' is a devastating comfort — she's essentially saying 'you've set the bar so low that even your absence is normal now.' Her matter-of-fact 'Yes, you do' when Andy says 'I suck' is pitch-perfect. This is Pam at her funniest — unfiltered honesty delivered without malice. The structure is excellent.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight IM each other while sitting near each other in the office. 'What are you writing about me?' 'I'm going to write you both up for not working.' — Jim and Dwight immediately turn it around to threaten to write each other up.
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are clearly goofing off by IMing each other
jokes.punchline: 'Well played. Neither of us will write the other up for not working.' — a perfect détente
jokes.explanation: 'Well played. Neither of us will write the other up for not working' is a great payoff — it formalizes their game of chicken into a peace treaty. The comedy of two people IMing while sitting near each other is also a nice visual (2008-era technology joke). Good character dynamic joke.

jokes.text: Michael is asking Holly if 'that guy' called. He overheard her conversation with Oscar. Holly: 'And you know what? I even got two tickets to see the Counting Crows tonight as a surprise. Why do guys not call when they say they're going to call?' Michael: 'I don't know. I always call everybody back right away.' — pause — 'But he'll call back, though. Give him until the end of the day. He'll call. He'll call. If he doesn't, he is loco.'
jokes.setup: Michael — who clearly has feelings for Holly — is counseling her about a guy who isn't calling her
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'I always call everybody back right away' as an implicit self-pitch, then desperately insisting 'he'll call, he'll call' while clearly hoping he won't; 'If he doesn't, he is loco' is the tell
jokes.explanation: Michael's performance of supportive friend while actually rooting for the guy to not call is layered character comedy. 'I always call everybody back right away' is Michael making a move while appearing to give friendly advice. 'He is loco' as his verdict on a man who doesn't call Holly is simultaneously genuine and self-serving.

jokes.text: Michael buys Holly's Counting Crows tickets from her and then asks if he can pay tomorrow because he has a $60 ATM limit.
jokes.setup: Holly has unused Counting Crows tickets for the guy who didn't call
jokes.punchline: Michael's impulse buy of the tickets is immediately undermined by his $60 ATM limit — he's trying to be smooth and is immediately broke-shamed
jokes.explanation: The romantic gesture immediately deflated by cash constraints is a nice beat. '$60 limit on my ATM' is the specific detail that makes it land. Michael trying to be a hero and immediately needing to ask for credit is very Michael.

jokes.text: The office turns on fans and heaters and runs in place to sweat out weight before the final weigh-in. Andy talking-head: 'Andy Bernard does not lose contests. He wins them. Or he quits them because they're unfair.'
jokes.setup: They're 8 pounds behind Utica with hours left
jokes.punchline: Andy's self-motivating speech undercut by '...or he quits them because they're unfair' — a perfectly self-aware caveat delivered without irony
jokes.explanation: One of the finest Andy Bernard lines ever written. The structure is a perfect two-beat joke: motivational declaration completely undermined by the exception clause. 'Or he quits them because they're unfair' is devastating because it's so specific (he has clearly done this before) and delivered with the same earnest conviction as the first clause. The self-awareness is totally absent — Andy genuinely sees quitting-because-it's-unfair as equivalent to winning. This is among the episode's best jokes and justifies high score. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Angela's first dance demand: 'The Little Drummer Boy.' Andy agrees immediately and reveals his a cappella group 'Here Comes Treble, class of '96' has been booked, will be the wedding band AND collectively his best man, and are crashing with them for three weeks.
jokes.setup: Andy asks Angela if their first dance can be to his favorite song
jokes.punchline: The escalating reveals: (1) The Little Drummer Boy as their first dance song; (2) the a cappella group is already booked; (3) they're collectively his best man; (4) they're staying with them for three weeks
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating sequence. Each revelation is worse than the last: a Christmas song as a first dance song, then the group is already non-refundably booked, then 'collectively my best man' (implying the entire 10+ person group shares the role), then three weeks of house guests. The escalation is well-constructed and each beat gets a reaction before the next lands.

jokes.text: Andy lists Here Comes Treble members: 'Carl I, Carl II, Broccoli Rob, Spare Rib, Doobie, Lunchbox. Boner Champ, that's me, Pubey Lewis and the News, Hopscotch, Jingle Jangle, Sandwich.'
jokes.setup: Andy is listing his a cappella group members
jokes.punchline: The nicknames escalate from mild ('Carl I, Carl II') to food-based ('Broccoli Rob, Spare Rib') to drug-adjacent ('Doobie') to crude ('Boner Champ' — and it's Andy's) to absurdist ('Pubey Lewis and the News, Hopscotch, Jingle Jangle, Sandwich')
jokes.explanation: One of the all-time great list jokes in The Office. The nicknames are a perfect comedy escalation: the two Carls establish normalcy, then Broccoli Rob starts the absurdity, then Doobie goes darker, Lunchbox pivots, and then the list becomes increasingly unhinged — 'Boner Champ, that's me' is a perfect self-insert where Andy identifies himself with quiet pride. 'Pubey Lewis and the News' is a masterwork of crude wordplay. 'Sandwich' as the final name — after all that — is the perfect anti-climax. The structure is brilliant: establish → escalate → peak → deflate. Among the best single jokes in this episode. 'Boner Champ, that's me' alone is television history. Justifies the highest craft score in the episode.

jokes.text: Jim proposes to Pam at a gas station in the rain, at the midpoint of their drives, because he can't wait.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam have been long-distance; they arranged a meet-up at a midpoint
jokes.punchline: The proposal happens at a gas station, in the rain — the anti-romantic setting is the joke, but it's played as genuinely romantic; the humor is in the gap between the grand gesture and the mundane setting
jokes.explanation: The gas station proposal is the emotional peak of the episode and also quietly funny — Jim's inability to wait for a 'proper' moment is consistent with his character, and the mundane setting is the joke. 'He didn't even do the math right — Montclair would have been closer' is the setup that makes the proposal funnier. The romance of a gas station proposal in the rain is Jim Halpert all over.

jokes.text: Office reaction to Jim and Pam's absence during the final weigh-in: 'God! Where is Jim?' — then the cut to the proposal reveal
jokes.setup: The office is doing its final desperate weigh-in effort
jokes.punchline: Michael is furious Jim is missing; the audience knows Jim is proposing — the juxtaposition of Michael's petty frustration and the romantic moment is the joke
jokes.explanation: A structural joke — the cutting between the proposal and the office's mundane panic creates comedic contrast. Works better in the episode than on the page.

jokes.text: Holly: 'I have to say, I think the problem with that whole thing... was that he was a complete stupid idiot.'
jokes.setup: Holly is processing why the guy didn't call
jokes.punchline: 'He was a complete stupid idiot' — delivered as a clinical analysis after a thoughtful setup pause
jokes.explanation: The setup pause before 'he was a complete stupid idiot' — Holly building to what sounds like a mature reflection and landing on a childish conclusion — is a good character beat. The redundancy of 'complete stupid idiot' (three intensifiers) is also a nice touch for Holly's character.

jokes.text: Michael's final motivational speech: 'I don't care what any stupid scale says, you guys are all gigantic losers.'
jokes.setup: The office failed to win the weight loss contest
jokes.punchline: 'You guys are all gigantic losers' — intended as a compliment (they lost weight = losers) but reading as an insult; Michael is unaware of the double meaning
jokes.explanation: Michael's accidental insult as compliment is a classic structure for this show. 'Gigantic losers' read in context of the weight-loss contest is a pun he doesn't intend. The earnestness of the preceding 'I don't care what any stupid scale says' makes it land harder. Quotable.

jokes.text: Michael talking-head: 'I don't know about anyone else, but it was a good summer for me. I lost seven pounds. And you know what? I'm just going to take five days off anyway.'
jokes.setup: The office lost the contest
jokes.punchline: Michael decides to take the vacation days anyway regardless of whether they won — the contest was only ever about Michael getting what he wanted
jokes.explanation: A good capper. Michael's casual 'I'm just going to take five days anyway' reveals that corporate rules apply to everyone except Michael in his own mind. The 'good summer for me' framing — when it was terrible for most others — is a nice self-centered observation.

jokes.text: Final tag: An unnamed character went zip lining in Costa Rica on day three, the harness wasn't strapped right, they broke their neck, have been in the hospital for five weeks, still haven't seen the beach, and 'It's nice to have visitors.'
jokes.setup: Episode closes with various characters' summer summaries
jokes.punchline: The escalating tragedy — zip lining → wrong harness → broken neck → five weeks in hospital → never saw the beach → 'It's nice to have visitors' — delivered with the same talking-head equanimity as 'I lost seven pounds'
jokes.explanation: A cold, dark, perfectly structured episode tag. The joke operates through structure: each revelation escalates the disaster (zip lining → harness not right → broke neck → five weeks hospitalized → still hasn't seen beach), and the final line — 'It's nice to have visitors' — is delivered with the same flat affect as everything else. The mundane positivity of 'nice to have visitors' against the backdrop of a broken neck from a Costa Rica vacation is devastatingly funny in its understatement. The structure mirrors the Office format perfectly: talking-head confession delivered as if the speaker lacks perspective on their own catastrophe. Justifies high score.

tmdb_overview: Michael tries to motivate the Scranton branch to lose weight as part of an interoffice competition. Jim is lost after Pam leaves for art school in New York, and Angela continues to see Dwight even though she is now engaged to Andy.
